trigger.fact: Kirk Maxey discussed why scientific validation remains essential as AI accelerates research in an August 2026 Cayman article.

reframe: AI should save scientists time finding evidence while keeping scientific validation with people.

contacts.name: Kirk Maxey
contacts.title: President & CEO
contacts.subject: AI your scientists can check
contacts.message:
Your ASP reflection made a useful distinction: faster discovery still needs scientific validation. I'd like to bring that same discipline to the work around the lab.

Nine-67 is an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers work with business and operations teams to build custom software. We recently helped one client deploy 20 applications.

We'd build a first version that helps staff find approved product evidence and prepare a sourced answer for a scientist to check. We'd measure research time saved, then train the team through launch.

Would it be useful to compare where your scientists spend time finding that evidence?

contacts.name: Stephen Barrett
contacts.title: VP, Innovation & Growth
contacts.subject: less digging before project reviews
contacts.message:
Your work spans Cayman's research partnerships, licensing and IP. An AI assistant could help pull the evidence for a project review together without handing scientific judgment to a model.

We're Nine-67, an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers learn the business alongside your team and build custom software around the work.

We'd build a review workspace that finds approved project evidence, links every answer to its source and leaves scientific validation with your people. We'd start with one review, measure preparation time, then refine it with the users.

Is preparing those reviews something you'd want help simplifying?

trigger.fact: Aaron Curtis described Alta's research linking cancellations to friction in the first days of customer onboarding. Alta already uses FieldRoutes.

reframe: The first days of customer onboarding are a chance to resolve friction before a cancellation.

contacts.name: Chris Langlois
contacts.title: CEO
contacts.subject: catching friction in week one
contacts.message:
Aaron Curtis's comments about cancellations starting in the first few days caught my attention. That gives an AI project a concrete job: help a branch act while the customer still wants things to work.

We're Nine-67, an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers work alongside operations teams to build custom software and get people using it.

We'd build on Alta's existing FieldRoutes setup, flagging onboarding friction from service notes for a manager to review. We'd measure how quickly those cases get resolved, then check whether fewer customers cancel.

Would an early-warning project for one branch be worth a conversation?

contacts.name: Aaron Curtis
contacts.title: Customer Experience Officer
contacts.subject: acting before the cancellation
contacts.message:
Your point about first-week friction being mistaken for price sensitivity is a good reason to put AI close to the service team. The useful moment is before a customer decides to cancel.

Nine-67 is an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers work with operations teams to build custom software and train the people using it.

We'd build a first pass that reads onboarding notes, groups recurring concerns and puts unresolved cases in front of the right branch manager. We'd work around FieldRoutes and compare resolution time with your current process.

Would you be open to walking through one of those early customer journeys?

contacts.subject: supplier updates and affected orders
contacts.message:
With Chrysan's teams across the US, Mexico and Asia, I'd explore one practical use for AI: turning a supplier's changed delivery date into a clear view of the orders it affects.

Is that a piece of work you'd like to make easier?

reframe: Production notes become useful when supervisors can connect a recurring interruption to a specific follow-up.

contacts.name: Jon DeArment
contacts.title: EVP, Manufacturing & Engineering
contacts.subject: AI on the shop floor
contacts.message:
Your move into manufacturing and engineering puts you close to where an AI tool has to earn its place: helping the people making the tools. I'd start with the production notes that supervisors already use.

We're Nine-67, an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers work alongside operations teams to build custom software and train the people using it.

We'd build a first version that groups recurring interruptions from those notes and tracks the agreed follow-up. We'd measure preparation time for shift reviews, with supervisors checking every conclusion.

Would you be open to comparing that with how your team runs a shift review?

contacts.name: Jimmy Bromley
contacts.title: President
contacts.subject: a practical AI starting point
contacts.message:
You put operational efficiency and financial discipline at the center of your introduction as Channellock's president. I'd like to explore an AI project you could judge on both.

Nine-67 is an AI-first company. Our forward-deployed engineers work with leaders and operations teams to build custom software. We recently helped one client deploy 20 applications.

We'd build around one production review: connect recurring interruptions in shift notes to the follow-up your supervisors agree on. We'd measure preparation time saved and whether actions get closed, then train the team through deployment.

Would a project like that be worth exploring with Jon?
